Meeting header:
Date: 2026-07-10
Start time: 15:00 PDT
Duration: ~42 mins
Attendees: Michael Chen (Redwood AE), Priya Kapoor (Redwood SE), Ana Gomez (Redwood Solutions), Lisa Martin (NovaRetail - Head of ML), David Park (NovaRetail - PM), Sanjay Rao (NovaRetail - Infra), Rachel Kim (NovaRetail - Security)

Summary (auto):
Quick hosted API demo covering chat/text generation basics: streaming responses, key parameters (temperature, top_p, max_tokens, stop), and retry/idempotency patterns. Discussed customer's constraints (latency <200ms for in-app suggestions, cost sensitivity, SOC2/compliance). Agreed to share pricing, streaming examples, and schedule a POC benchmark.

Topics:
- Hosted API capabilities (chat + text endpoints)
- Streaming: how to wire up client-side streaming and partial renders
- Parameters & best practices for quality/cost tradeoffs
- Retries / idempotency / backoff patterns for 429/5xx
- Security & compliance (SOC2, KMS, VPC options for Dedicated)
- Next steps: trial key, sample prompts, benchmark run

--- Transcript ---
[00:00] Michael Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, uh, appreciate you making time. Quick intros from Redwood, I'm Michael Chen, AE, Priya is our SE, Ana on solutions. Could you go around quickly?
[00:07] Lisa Martin: Sure, Lisa Martin, Head of ML at NovaRetail. We're building a shopping assistant and wanna evaluate hosted inference for chat responses and short product descriptions.
[00:12] David Park: David Park, product. We're primarily focused on in-app latency and cost per API call.
[00:16] Sanjay Rao: Sanjay, infra. I'm here for security/networking questions.
[00:20] Rachel Kim: Rachel, security, focusing on compliance and logs.
[00:23] Priya Kapoor: Great, thanks. We'll do a short demo of the hosted chat/text endpoints, show streaming, explain params and then go into retry strategies. Feel free to interrupt.

[02:10] Priya Kapoor: Ok starting the demo — at a high level Redwood's hosted API provides chat and text generation. The endpoint looks similar to /v1/chat/completions, streaming supported via server-sent events or websocket. You'll get incremental tokens and can render partial answers in the UI which is great for perceived latency.
[03:05] David Park: Quick question — when you say streaming, are we able to stream and show partial product titles in the UI while the model is still generating?
[03:12] Priya Kapoor: Yes, exactly. You can render tokens as they arrive — that means the user's first visible token can be within tens to low hundreds of ms depending on network and model. We demo with a small friendly model; for production you'd pick a model that meets your 95th percentile latency SLO.

[04:00] Michael Chen: Lisa earlier mentioned a target of sub-200ms on interactive suggestions, is that still accurate?
[04:07] Lisa Martin: Yeah that's our goal for the top suggestions; we can accept slightly higher for full paragraphs but suggestions should feel instant.

[05:15] Priya Kapoor: For sub-200ms interactive use cases we often do: compact models + streaming + prefix caching. Redwood supports KV cache (sometimes transcribed in logs as K V cash) so repeated prefixes are served quickly. Also you can use shorter max_tokens for suggestion endpoints. Example params: temperature 0.2-0.6 for deterministic suggestions, top_p 0.9, max_tokens 24-80 depending on UI.

[06:40] David Park: Can you show the actual request and the streaming SSE?
[06:45] Priya Kapoor: Yep, here's a simplified example we pasted in the demo deck — POST /v1/chat/completions with a streaming header. Then you read chunked events, each contains delta pieces like: {"role":"assistant","content":{"delta":"The product is..."}} — the transcript generator sometimes changes formatting but the pattern is standard.

[08:22] Priya Kapoor: Important client patterns: use an idempotency key for submissions that change state, and on 429/5xx use exponential backoff with jitter. Redwood's client SDKs include helpers; example backoff: initial 200ms, 2x multiply, jitter 0-100ms, cap at 5s. For long-running bursts try queuing client-side and stream partials back to UI.

[09:55] Sanjay Rao: If we see a 429, is it per-API-key limit or per-IP? How do we surface rate-limits?
[10:02] Michael Chen: Rate limits are per-account keys and per-route; in hosted we'll supply headers with remaining quota and a Retry-After where appropriate. We can also configure higher quotas for trials or a dedicated pool under Redwood Dedicated.

[11:40] Rachel Kim: On security — SOC2 and encryption at rest?
[11:44] Michael Chen: Yes, Redwood is SOC2 compliant; we support customer-managed keys via KMS/HSM for Private deployments but hosted also encrypts at rest and in transit. We keep audit logs, RBAC in the console, and can provide the security pack. We'll share the security docs after the call.

[13:00] Priya Kapoor: Back to params — a few tradeoffs: higher temperature increases creativity but can reduce determinism for product descriptions; increase top_p to broaden sampling. For cost savings use lower max_tokens and experiment with quantized model variants (we can recommend model+quantization combo in Redwood Optimize). Also batching on the client if you have many small writes—Redwood Optimize suggests batching policies.

[15:25] David Park: What about retries and idempotency for streaming responses — if a stream fails mid response, what's the recommended approach?
[15:30] Priya Kapoor: Two patterns: 1) Client resumes with the last committed token and request a completion from that prefix — but that requires you keep the prefix on client. 2) Use idempotency keys for server-side dedup but note streaming partials are not re-playable automatically. We often run short lived completions and on failure re-request with same idempotency key; server can detect duplicates for non-streaming calls. For streaming, best to checkpoint at UI level and request the remainder or restart generation with the user-visible prefix.

[17:05] Michael Chen: For NovaRetail, given you want sub-200ms suggestions, we usually recommend a small low-latency hosted model with streaming + KV cache for repeats. If you want absolute predictability and dedicated capacity you can move to Redwood Dedicated (reserved GPU pool) — that also gives options for private network egress and stricter SLAs.

[19:30] Lisa Martin: Is there a difference in data retention between hosted and dedicated? We need logs for debugging but can't retain user PII beyond 30 days.
[19:36] Michael Chen: Hosted defaults to short retention but you can request different retention windows with enterprise contracts; Private deployments give you full control. We'll include retention options in the security doc.

[21:00] Priya Kapoor: Showing console briefly — you can view per-route latency, token counts, costs, and rollouts. For instance, you can run a canary on a new model, route 5% traffic, and use automatic fallback to a cheaper variant if latency SLOs aren't met.

[23:10] David Park: For the UI we might call suggestions endpoint as user types. Would client-side debounce plus streaming be the right pattern?
[23:18] Priya Kapoor: Yes, debounce on keystroke to reduce calls, keep a short prefix and stream tokens as they arrive. Also use a low max_tokens for suggestions and an async longer completion for full descriptions. That splits cost and keeps interactive feel.

[25:45] Sanjay Rao: For outbound connections from our VPC are there known IP ranges we need to allowlist for hosted?
[25:50] Michael Chen: For hosted we provide an allowlist bundle of egress IPs and we can also offer a proxy option; if you need full network isolation we recommend Redwood Private or Dedicated with VPC egress. We'll follow up with the exact CIDRs.

[27:20] Rachel Kim: How do you handle PII and redaction?
[27:25] Michael Chen: We support PII scrubbing in the pipeline (we can surface redaction hooks) and for regulated data we recommend Private with customer-managed keys. Hosted has standard redaction options documented, but we'll share the SOC2 pack and our redaction best practices doc.

[29:10] Priya Kapoor: Quick note on metrics: you can track per-token cost, 95th/99th latency, per-route error rates. Redwood Optimize will recommend model variants and quantization levels to hit cost/latency targets based on real traffic.

[31:00] Lisa Martin: Curious about fallback — if our chosen model becomes unavailable is there an automatic fallback to a smaller model?
[31:06] Priya Kapoor: Yes, smart routing can fallback to compatible model variants by policy — for example route by latency then cost, fallback to a quantized variant or older checkpoint. That keeps your UI alive.

[33:20] David Park: Can you share example retries code?
[33:25] Priya Kapoor: Sure — here's a pseudocode snippet: try request -> if 429 or 503 then sleep(backoff + jitter) and retry up to N times; on 5xx you might also circuit-break after repeated failures. We have SDK helpers and best-practice docs, I'll share the exact snippet.

[35:55] Michael Chen: Ok wrapping up — key recommendations: for NovaRetail interactive suggestions start with hosted small model + streaming + KV cache, monitor with Console, and use Redwood Optimize recommendations. If predictable throughput or strict network isolation is required use Dedicated or Private.

[36:30] Lisa Martin: That sounds good. Timelines: we want to run a short POC next week with 1k sample prompts and measure 95th percentile latency.

[36:38] Michael Chen: Great. Action items captured — we'll send a trial key, pricing, security pack, streaming example and retry patterns.

[38:00] Sanjay Rao: One more nit — do you support SAML SSO and SCIM for user provisioning?
[38:05] Michael Chen: Yes SAML and SCIM supported for console access, RBAC can be enforced. We'll include setup steps in the security doc.

[39:20] Rachel Kim: Also please include what logs are available for audit and how long they're retained by default.
[39:25] Michael Chen: Will include.

[40:10] David Park: Any rough ballpark on cost for hosted suggestions — like per 1k requests for a small model?
[40:15] Michael Chen: Ballpark in email, but expect hosted to be competitive vs major APIs; we'll put line items in the proposal.

[41:00] Michael Chen: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up end of day with the docs and trial key and Priya will send the code snippets.

End of transcript.
